samples: This program requests a customers endpoint over HTTP, following each page's "next cursor" until the API stops returning one, and gathers all customers into one list. It then groups them by country and prints one line per country with its customer count, largest first. It only reads data (network access plus console output), but it has no page limit and does not URL-encode the cursor, so a misbehaving API that keeps returning cursors would make it loop indefinitely, and the grouping step is written in a form the language reference doesn't show, so check that it compiles before relying on it.

This program fetches every page of customers from an example API at a fixed address, following the "next page" cursor each response gives until none is returned, then prints each country with its customer count, largest first. It needs network access and console output, and it stops with an HTTP or JSON error if a request fails or a response can't be parsed, with no retries, delays, or limits on how many pages it fetches. One caution: the grouping step doesn't end with a collect or sum clause as the cheat sheet's examples do, and it builds the next-page address by inserting the base address into text, so I can't confirm from the cheat sheet that those lines are valid as written.

This program calls a customer API at a hardcoded example address, following each page's "next" cursor until the API stops returning one, and collects all the customer records. It then prints one line per country with the number of customers there, largest count first. It needs network access and console output, and any HTTP or JSON-parsing failure on any page aborts the whole run with no partial results. One caveat: the grouping step in the main function appears to lack the "collect" or "sum" ending the cheat sheet shows for group queries, so check that it compiles before relying on it.

This program downloads every customer from a cursor-paginated web API by requesting page after page until the API stops returning a "next" cursor, and then prints how many customers each country has, largest first. It needs network access and console output, and it fails with an HTTP or JSON error if a request or response parse goes wrong, so a failure on any page means no partial results are printed. Before relying on it, note that the endpoint is hardcoded to an example address, so you would need to change that, and it appends the cursor to the address without encoding it, which may matter if your API uses an unusual cursor format or its address already has query parameters.

This program calls a customer API at a fixed example address, following each page's "next" cursor until the API stops returning one. It collects all customers, then prints each country with its customer count, largest first. It needs network access and console output, fails if the HTTP request or JSON decoding fails, and has no page limit or timeout, so a misbehaving API that keeps returning cursors would make it loop forever. The grouping step in the main function omits the collect or sum ending that the cheat sheet's grouping examples all show, so check that it compiles and behaves as intended before relying on it.
